lines: Notice that nothing here looks broken from either customer's point of view.
Each one gets a clean confirmation. The system did exactly what it was built to do: keep answering, even while it couldn't talk to the other side.
That's the cost about to get named, not a bug report.
Before choosing, ask what the isolated side was actually free to do differently.
It could have refused the sale instead of confirming it. That refusal is the only alternative on the table once the network splits.
answer: It kept availability, at the cost of consistency.
Every node kept responding right through the partition, and that's precisely what let both sides confirm the same unit.
Refusing on the isolated side was the one path not taken.

lines: Hold these three conditions apart, because the proof only works if you don't blur them.
Atomic is a statement about order appearing instantaneous. Available is a statement about never staying silent. Partition tolerant is a statement about how much message loss the network is allowed.
The theorem's whole claim is that a design can't satisfy all three at once.
Watch what the isolated replica can and can't know, not what actually happened elsewhere.
It never receives the majority's write, so its own local state looks exactly the same whether that write occurred or not.
Given no fact to tell the two worlds apart, any answer it gives is either a refusal or a gamble.
Separate the thing that happens to a system from the thing the system decides.
A partition isn't a decision anyone makes; it's an event. The decision is what to do once one is already underway, and that decision gets made fresh for each request.
A label stamped on the whole system can't capture something that granular.
Notice this trade-off exists even on a day with no partition at all.
Replicating a write before answering costs time, so a system still has to pick between answering fast and answering with full consistency, partition or not.
Three real systems sit in three different corners of that choice, each by its own design.
Pay attention to which word is doing the real work in that sentence: effectively.
Technically, Spanner gives up availability during a partition, same as any CP system has to.
What changes is how rarely that moment arrives on a network built and run by one company end to end.
Carry forward the shape of the whole argument, not just three letters that rhyme.
One theorem about a single moment of indecision. One else-branch about every other moment. One real system that pays the theorem's cost rarely, not never.
Before answering, ask what the theorem is actually a claim about: a design, or a track record.
A system that has gotten lucky still carries a choice baked into its design for the day a partition finally arrives.
answer: The theorem constrains what a design has to give up if a partition occurs, and says nothing about how often that will happen.
Years without one is a fact about history, not a property the design has that gets it out of the trade.
